newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Washington starts Middle East rescue mission.
newsitem.headline: Washington starts Middle East rescue mission.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton's special envoy began a Middle East rescue mission in Morocco on Thursday by charting peace moves with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
Veteran mediator Dennis Ross arrived in the Moroccan capital Rabat late on Wednesday at the start of a lightning bid to get Israelis and Palestinians to stop fighting and start talking.
"There is a message with Dennis Ross from President Clinton...We shall see," Arafat told reporters when he flew into Morocco to meet Ross and attend an Islamic meeting on Jerusalem.
It was unclear when Ross and Arafat would meet.

Israel said Ross would meet Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at his Jerusalem home at 2030 GMT later in the day, and again at Netanyahu's office at 0930 GMT on Friday, joined by Israel's foreign and defence ministers.
In Rabat, Ross told Reuters he would return to Washington by the weekend to report to Clinton so the "president can decide what the next proper move should be."

Israel's groundbreaking on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem has ignited eight days of violence including clashes between Israeli troops and Palestinian stone-throwers and the killing of three Israeli women last Friday by a Palestinian suicide bomber who blew himself up at a Tel Aviv cafe.

Asked what influence Ross would have on the two sides, Uri Saguy, a former Israeli military intelligence chief said: "About as much as aspirin has on flu -- it is marginal and brings the fever down a bit but it doesn't cure the ailment itself."

In the West Bank town of Bir Zeit on Thursday, about 70 Palestinian youths hurled stones at Israeli border policemen who responded with teargas and rubber bullets. Witnesses said Palestinian security forces restrained the stone-throwers.
Israel's Defence Ministry said the army would station tanks at the outskirts of Palestinian-ruled cities if needed to deter stone-throwing demonstrators from charging soldiers at Israeli outposts.

Israeli political analysts said Ross faced as tall an order as he did last year when -- after a wave of violence claimed the lives of 61 Palestinians and 15 Israelis -- he brokered Israel's handover of most of Hebron to self-rule.

Analysts said he could devise a formula by which Arafat would recommit to fight violence and Netanyahu would promise not to take any more unilateral steps such as last week's Jewish settlement groundbreaking.

Palestinians are also angry over Netanyahu's decision to limit a March 17 handover to Palestinian self-rule to only nine percent of the West Bank. Arafat's Palestinian Authority wanted three times as much territory.
Israel said Ross must press the Palestinian Authority to crack down on Moslem militant groups.

Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh told Israeli army radio that events had cast "a very dark shadow" over the future of peacemaking with the Palestinians, insisting he was unaware of any demands the United States might place on Israel.
Palestinian officials urged Ross to lean on Israel to halt work on the East Jerusalem hilltop which the Arabs call Jabal Abu Ghneim and the Israelis call Har Homa.
The Israeli housing project enraged Palestinians who regard East Jerusalem, occupied by Israel in the 1967 Middle East War, as the future capital of an independent Palestinian state.
Arafat was in Rabat to join 15 foreign ministers from Islamic countries at a meeting of the Jerusalem Committee called by Morocco's King Hassan over Israel's new settlement project.
The Jerusalem Committee, headed by the king, was set up by an Islamic Conference Organisation summit in 1975 to try to prevent Israel from making any demographic changes to Jerusalem.

At the United Nations, the Arab group of states planned to request an emergency special session of the General Assembly on Israel's building of homes for Jews in East Jerusalem following two U.S. vetoes in the Security Council.
